Recall \(\wedge\) = switches in series, \(\vee\) = branches in parallel.

The expression is \((\sim p \wedge q) \vee (p \wedge \sim r)\), a parallel combination of two branches.

Branch 1 \((\sim p \wedge q)\): switch \(S_1'\) (closed when \(p\)'s switch is open) in series with switch \(S_2\) (for \(q\)).

Branch 2 \((p \wedge \sim r)\): switch \(S_1\) (for \(p\)) in series with switch \(S_3'\) (closed when \(r\)'s switch is open).

The two branches are connected in parallel between the terminals of the lamp.

Here \(\wedge\) = series and \(\vee\) = parallel.

The expression \((p \wedge q) \vee [\sim p \wedge (\sim q \vee p \vee r)]\) is a parallel combination of two branches.

Branch 1 \((p \wedge q)\): switch \(S_1\) (for \(p\)) in series with switch \(S_2\) (for \(q\)).

Branch 2 \(\sim p \wedge (\sim q \vee p \vee r)\): switch \(S_1'\) (closed when \(p\) is open) in series with a parallel sub-network of three switches \(S_2'\) (for \(\sim q\)), \(S_1\) (for \(p\)) and \(S_3\) (for \(r\)).

The two branches are joined in parallel across the supply.

Here \(\wedge\) = series and \(\vee\) = parallel.

The expression \([(p \wedge r) \vee (\sim q \wedge \sim r)] \wedge (\sim p \wedge \sim r)\) is a series combination of two blocks.

Block 1 \((p \wedge r) \vee (\sim q \wedge \sim r)\): two parallel branches — one branch is \(S_1\) (for \(p\)) in series with \(S_3\) (for \(r\)); the other branch is \(S_2'\) (for \(\sim q\)) in series with \(S_3'\) (for \(\sim r\)).

Block 2 \((\sim p \wedge \sim r)\): switch \(S_1'\) (for \(\sim p\)) in series with switch \(S_3'\) (for \(\sim r\)).

Block 1 and Block 2 are then connected in series with each other.

Here \(\wedge\) = series and \(\vee\) = parallel.

The expression \((p \wedge \sim q \wedge r) \vee [p \wedge (\sim q \vee \sim r)]\) is a parallel combination of two branches.

Branch 1 \((p \wedge \sim q \wedge r)\): three switches in series — \(S_1\) (for \(p\)), \(S_2'\) (for \(\sim q\)) and \(S_3\) (for \(r\)).

Branch 2 \(p \wedge (\sim q \vee \sim r)\): switch \(S_1\) (for \(p\)) in series with a parallel sub-network of \(S_2'\) (for \(\sim q\)) and \(S_3'\) (for \(\sim r\)).

The two branches are connected in parallel across the supply.

Here \(\wedge\) = series and \(\vee\) = parallel.

The expression \(p \vee (\sim p) \vee (\sim q) \vee (p \wedge q)\) is a parallel combination of four branches.

Branch 1: switch \(S_1\) (for \(p\)).

Branch 2: switch \(S_1'\) (for \(\sim p\)).

Branch 3: switch \(S_2'\) (for \(\sim q\)).

Branch 4 \((p \wedge q)\): switch \(S_1\) (for \(p\)) in series with switch \(S_2\) (for \(q\)).

All four branches are connected in parallel across the supply.

(Note: since a branch containing \(p\) and a branch containing \(\sim p\) are already in parallel, this circuit is always closed.)

Here \(\wedge\) = series and \(\vee\) = parallel.

The expression \((p \wedge q) \vee (\sim p) \vee (p \wedge \sim q)\) is a parallel combination of three branches.

Branch 1 \((p \wedge q)\): switch \(S_1\) (for \(p\)) in series with switch \(S_2\) (for \(q\)).

Branch 2: switch \(S_1'\) (for \(\sim p\)).

Branch 3 \((p \wedge \sim q)\): switch \(S_1\) (for \(p\)) in series with switch \(S_2'\) (for \(\sim q\)).

The three branches are connected in parallel across the supply.

Simplify \(p \vee (q \wedge \sim q)\).

By the complement law, \(q \wedge \sim q \equiv F\).

Hence \(p \vee (q \wedge \sim q) \equiv p \vee F \equiv p\) (identity law).

Simplified expression: \(p\).

Switching circuit: a single switch \(S_1\) (for \(p\)) connected in series with the lamp across the supply.

Simplify \((\sim p \wedge q) \vee (\sim p \wedge \sim q) \vee (p \wedge \sim q)\).

Take \(\sim p\) common from the first two terms:
\((\sim p \wedge q) \vee (\sim p \wedge \sim q) \equiv \sim p \wedge (q \vee \sim q) \equiv \sim p \wedge T \equiv \sim p\).

So the expression \(\equiv \sim p \vee (p \wedge \sim q)\).

By the distributive law, \(\sim p \vee (p \wedge \sim q) \equiv (\sim p \vee p) \wedge (\sim p \vee \sim q) \equiv T \wedge (\sim p \vee \sim q) \equiv \sim p \vee \sim q\).

Simplified expression: \(\sim p \vee \sim q\).

Switching circuit: two switches \(S_1'\) (for \(\sim p\)) and \(S_2'\) (for \(\sim q\)) connected in parallel across the supply.

Simplify \([p \vee (\sim q) \vee \sim r] \wedge [p \vee (q \wedge r)]\).

Write it as \((p \vee X) \wedge (p \vee Y)\) with \(X = \sim q \vee \sim r\) and \(Y = q \wedge r\). By the distributive law,
\((p \vee X) \wedge (p \vee Y) \equiv p \vee (X \wedge Y)\).

Now by De Morgan's law \(\sim q \vee \sim r \equiv \sim(q \wedge r)\), so
\(X \wedge Y \equiv \sim(q \wedge r) \wedge (q \wedge r) \equiv F\) (complement law).

Hence the expression \(\equiv p \vee F \equiv p\).

Simplified expression: \(p\).

Switching circuit: a single switch \(S_1\) (for \(p\)) connected in series with the lamp across the supply.

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed answer key gives \((q \wedge r) \vee p\); the correct simplification is \(r \wedge (p \vee q)\) (our answer).]

Simplify \((p \wedge q \wedge \sim p) \vee (\sim p \wedge q \wedge r) \vee (p \wedge \sim q \wedge r) \vee (p \wedge q \wedge r)\).

First term: \(p \wedge \sim p \equiv F\), so \(p \wedge q \wedge \sim p \equiv F\) and it is dropped.

Combine the 1st and 3rd remaining terms (which share \(q \wedge r\)):
\((\sim p \wedge q \wedge r) \vee (p \wedge q \wedge r) \equiv (q \wedge r) \wedge (\sim p \vee p) \equiv q \wedge r\).

So the expression \(\equiv (q \wedge r) \vee (p \wedge \sim q \wedge r)\). Take \(r\) common:
\(\equiv r \wedge [q \vee (p \wedge \sim q)]\).

Now \(q \vee (p \wedge \sim q) \equiv (q \vee p) \wedge (q \vee \sim q) \equiv (p \vee q) \wedge T \equiv p \vee q\).

Hence the expression \(\equiv (p \vee q) \wedge r\).

Simplified expression: \((p \vee q) \wedge r\).

Switching circuit: switches \(S_1\) (for \(p\)) and \(S_2\) (for \(q\)) in parallel, and this parallel combination is connected in series with switch \(S_3\) (for \(r\)).
